![Restore a Joomla backup using Docker](/img/v2/joomla.webp)

<TLDR>
  This guide explains how to restore a Joomla site locally by combining Docker,
  an Akeeba Backup archive, and the Akeeba Kickstart utility. Users configure a
  custom environment with PHP and Apache, then execute a simple import command
  to deploy the necessary files and containers. The process is completed by
  accessing the Kickstart wizard in a browser to finalize the database
  connection and site restoration.
</TLDR>

In previous articles ([Part 1](/blog/docker-joomla) and [Part 2](/blog/docker-joomla-part-2)), we've seen how to create a Joomla site from scratch by using Docker: pull Joomla, PHP, Apache and MySQL from Docker Hub and do magic stuff so we have a fresh `http://127.0.0.1:8080` local site.

In this article, we'll see how to restore on our machine, a backup created thanks to great **[Akeeba Backup](https://www.akeeba.com/products/akeeba-backup.html)** component.

We'll reuse some files from [Part 2](/blog/docker-joomla-part-2) and make some changes to them.

At the end, we'll have a `make import` command that will start **[Akeeba Kickstart](https://www.akeeba.com/download.html#kickstart)**.

<!-- truncate -->

## Result

Fill in the database info shown in your console, and Akeeba Kickstart takes care of the rest —
from a raw `.jpa` backup to a browsable site:

![Akeeba Kickstart](./images/kickstart.webp)

![Restoring the database](./images/database.webp)

![Site is restored](./images/site_is_restored.webp)

## Why it works

- We reuse the same `compose.yaml`/`.env`/`makefile` trio from [Part 2](/blog/docker-joomla-part-2), so nothing new to learn there.
- The only real change: since the backup already **is** a full Joomla site, the containers only need PHP and Apache, not a fresh Joomla image — the database itself gets rebuilt from the backup by Akeeba Kickstart, not by Joomla's installer.

## Creating required files

<AlertBox variant="info" title="Skipping the files creation process">
In the next chapters, you'll need to create several files using copy/paste. If you wish to go faster, just run the following commands to retrieve files from my [Github repo](https://github.com/cavo789/docker_joomla_restore) so you don't need to create them.

<Terminal typewriter source="./files/terminal-3.txt" />

By following the instructions below, you'll create a xxx folder where you can copy all the files you need to restore a Joomla site using Docker. You can then proceed immediately to the “Run the import process” chapter, as the files are already in place.

</AlertBox>

_If you prefer to understand what you do and create files manually, please continue reading below._

Please create a new folder on your computer like f.i. `mkdir /tmp/joomla_restore && cd $_`.

<Terminal typewriter>$ mkdir /tmp/joomla_restore && cd $_</Terminal>

In that folder, you'll need to create several files (please refer to [Part 2](/blog/docker-joomla-part-2)) if you need more explanations about these files.

### The orchestration file: compose.yaml

Below, highlighted, small differences from the `compose.yaml` file we saw in [Part 2](/blog/docker-joomla-part-2#updated-composeyaml).

Here is why: this time we don't need to download a fresh copy of Joomla since **we already have a Joomla site** (our backup). What we need is **PHP** and **Apache**. We don't need Joomla, so this time we'll use a custom Docker image, not an already existing one.

Except for the highlighted lines, everything else is the same as in [Part 2](/blog/docker-joomla-part-2).

<Snippet filename="compose.yaml" source="./files/compose.yaml" />

### The .env file

As introduced above, we don't need Joomla anymore, just PHP and Apache. We'll then define a `PHP_VERSION` variable and initialize it to the desired version.

<Snippet filename=".env" source="./files/.env" />

<AlertBox variant="caution">
Since we need to restore an existing site, make sure to use the same PHP version as the one used by your site.

</AlertBox>

### Our makefile

We'll need a new action called `import`:

<Snippet filename="makefile" source="./files/makefile" />

<AlertBox variant="caution">
If you don't know if you already have `GNU make`, just run `which make` in the console. If you see `make not found` then please run `sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install make` to proceed with the installation.

<Terminal typewriter>$ which make</Terminal>

<Terminal typewriter>$ sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install make</Terminal>

</AlertBox>

### We also need a file called Dockerfile

In the very first lines of the `compose.yaml` file we've this portion:

<Snippet filename="compose.yaml" source="./files/compose_dockerfile.yaml" />

We don't see here an `image:` statement but a `build:` one. This means that we need a special file called `Dockerfile`.

Please create a new file called `Dockerfile` in your folder with this content:

<Snippet filename="Dockerfile" source="./files/Dockerfile" />

That file is quite simple right now: it tells us we need a PHP Docker image, and we also need to install the `mysqli` drivers.

### We need a backup for sure

Please also put a backup of your existing site and save it in the same folder. For standardization needs, please call that file `backup.jpa`.

To make this step more explicit: jump to your existing Joomla website and, using Akeeba Backup, create a backup (file format: `.jpa`) and download the backup. Please rename the backup file like this: `backup.jpa`.

### And finally, we need Akeeba Kickstart

Finally, we also need to have two files coming from **[Akeeba Kickstart](https://www.akeeba.com/download.html#kickstart)**.

By following the link [Akeeba Kickstart](https://www.akeeba.com/download.html#kickstart), we'll be able to download a `.zip` file (called `kickstart-core-xxx.zip` where `xxx` is a version number). Proceed to the download and open the archives: we'll get two files in it. Please copy these files in your folder.

The two files we need are called `en-GB.kickstart.ini` and `kickstart.php`.

## Before starting

We're ready. Just before you begin, please check that you have all the required files (please run `ls -alh`):

<Terminal typewriter source="./files/terminal-2.txt" />

<AlertBox variant="info" title="Skipping the files creation process">
If you've skipped the file creation step earlier by downloading files from my repo, you'll have all the files listed above.

</AlertBox>

<AlertBox variant="caution">
Remember, for Linux users, we need `GNU make` to be able to run commands like `make import` or `make up`. If you see `make not found` then please run `sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install make` to proceed with the installation.

</AlertBox>

## Run the importation process

Ok, you've copied a lot of files. Time to start restoring your site.

For Linux users, simply take advantage of `GNU Make` and run the `make import` instruction.

For Windows (Powershell or DOS), please run these commands:

<Terminal typewriter title="Powershell">
  mkdir db_data mkdir joomla_data copy en-GB.kickstart.ini joomla_data\ copy
  kickstart.php joomla_data\ copy backup.jpa joomla_data\ docker compose up
  --detach
</Terminal>

For both users (Linux and Windows), you'll get something like this output in the console:

<Terminal typewriter source="./files/terminal-1.txt" />

When finished, just start your browser and surf to `http://127.0.0.1:8080/kickstart.php` to start the restoration of your website using the **Akeeba Kickstart** wizard — the screens shown at the top of this article.

Once you need to fill in the database information, please refer to what was displayed in your console.

Continue the restoration as you always have; close the window once Akeeba Kickstart asks for it, then click on the _Clean Up_ button; then on _Visit your site's frontend_ and enjoy.

<AlertBox variant="info">
If you've used the provided demo site, the admin account is **joomla** and its password is **joomla@secured**.

</AlertBox>

## Conclusion

As we've just seen, restoring a Joomla site locally has become really simple.

All you need to do is retrieve a few configuration files, and just the one named `.env` should be updated with the PHP and MySQL versions you're using on your production site.

You download the local backup of your site and, with a single command (`make import`), your site is restored.

<Terminal typewriter>$ make import</Terminal>

No matter what version of Joomla or MySQL you're using.

Piece of cake, no?
